gloss_terse: Yivniyah, a Benjamite mentioned in 1 Chronicles 9:8
gloss_readable: This personal name appears once in the genealogical records of returning exiles. The name likely derives from a root meaning 'Yah builds' or 'Yah understands,' though the exact etymology remains uncertain. The Septuagint renders it as Banaia in some manuscripts and Iechoniou in the Lucianic recension, reflecting the textual ambiguity surrounding rare proper names in Chronicles.

senses.1: A Benjamite ancestral figure listed among the post-exilic inhabitants of Jerusalem (1 Chr 9:8). The single occurrence and lack of further narrative detail suggest this is a genealogical marker rather than a developed character, typical of Chronicles' compression of tribal lists.

gloss_terse: Jeberechiah, father of the witness Zechariah in Isaiah 8:2
gloss_readable: This Yahwistic theophoric name means 'Yah has blessed' and appears in its full form only once, though the abbreviated form Berechiah occurs for several different individuals throughout the Old Testament. Isaiah summons Jeberechiah's son Zechariah as a reliable witness to the prophetic oracle concerning Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz. The name's meaning underscores the divine favor associated with this witness's lineage.

senses.1: The father of Zechariah, one of two faithful witnesses called by Isaiah to attest to the prophet's written oracle (Isa 8:2). The full theophoric form (Jeberechiah) emphasizes the witness's credibility through association with divine blessing, strengthening the prophetic testimony.

gloss_terse: Yivsam, a descendant of Issachar in 1 Chronicles 7:2
gloss_readable: This personal name appears in the genealogical register of Issachar's descendants. The name's etymology is uncertain, though it may relate to sweetness or fragrance. Like many names in the tribal genealogies of Chronicles, this individual receives no narrative development beyond being listed as part of the ancestral lineage.

senses.1: A son or descendant of Tola from the tribe of Issachar, mentioned in the genealogical listing of warriors and clan heads (1 Chr 7:2). The conjunction indicates this name is part of a series enumerating Tola's sons, suggesting a genealogical rather than narrative function.

gloss_terse: Aramaic word for 'earth' or 'dry land' in Daniel 2:10
gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun, cognate with Hebrew yabbāšāh (dry land), appears in the Chaldeans' response to Nebuchadnezzar. The context emphasizes the vast gulf between human and divine knowledge: no magician 'on the earth' can reveal the king's dream. The Targum equates this term with the standard Biblical Hebrew for dry land, underscoring its semantic overlap with the Genesis creation narrative's 'dry ground' that emerges from the waters.

senses.1: The earth or inhabited world as the realm of human existence, contrasted with the divine sphere (Dan 2:10). The Chaldeans use this term to stress that no earthly wise man possesses the supernatural knowledge the king demands, highlighting the impossibility of the request.

gloss_terse: Plowmen, agricultural laborers (Jeremiah 52:16)
gloss_readable: This rare verbal form refers to those who till the soil and work the land. It appears in the context of Nebuzaradan leaving behind the poorest of the land after the Babylonian conquest to serve as vinedressers and plowmen. The parallel passage in 2 Kings 25:12 has a different reading in the Ketiv-Qere tradition, suggesting some textual fluidity. The agricultural role represents the most basic subsistence labor assigned to those too poor to be carried into exile.

senses.1: Agricultural workers who plow and cultivate fields, mentioned alongside vinedressers as the poorest inhabitants left in Judah after the exile (Jer 52:16). The term designates manual laborers who remained to maintain basic agricultural production while the skilled and wealthy were deported.

gloss_terse: Fields, agricultural plots (Jeremiah 39:10)
gloss_readable: This noun denotes cultivated land or fields, though the text in Jeremiah 39:10 presents some uncertainty. The word appears alongside vineyards in the description of what Nebuzaradan distributed to the poor who remained in Judah. The parallel passage in Jeremiah 52:16 offers a slightly different reading, and BDB notes the text is dubious. The agricultural context is clear: these are productive parcels of land suitable for cultivation.

senses.1: Cultivated fields or agricultural plots given to the poorest people left in the land after the Babylonian conquest (Jer 39:10). The distribution of vineyards and fields to those who had owned nothing represents a social upheaval where the dispossessed inherited the property of the exiled.

gloss_terse: Yigdalyahu, a prophet during Josiah's reign (Jeremiah 35:4)
gloss_readable: This theophoric name means 'Yah is great' and belongs to a man of God mentioned in connection with the Rechabites. Jeremiah brings the Rechabite family to a chamber in the temple belonging to the sons of Yigdalyahu, suggesting this prophet held some official position or owned property within the temple complex. The name reflects the common Yahwistic naming pattern celebrating God's greatness.

senses.1: A prophet or 'man of God' whose sons had a chamber in the Jerusalem temple where Jeremiah tested the Rechabites' faithfulness (Jer 35:4). The association with temple chambers suggests Yigdalyahu held recognized prophetic authority or priestly status during the reign of Josiah.

gloss_terse: To thrust away or remove (2 Samuel 20:13)
gloss_readable: This rare Hiphil verb describes the action of forcibly removing or pushing something aside. It appears only once, when someone thrust the murdered Amasa's body off the highway after Joab had killed him. The parallel clause uses a more common verb for carrying or turning aside, suggesting this term emphasizes the forceful, perhaps undignified nature of removing the corpse from public view. Arabic and Syriac cognates carry similar meanings of repelling or expelling.

senses.1: The act of forcibly thrusting or pushing away Amasa's body from the road where it lay after Joab's assassination (2 Sam 20:13). The vigorous action was necessary to prevent the pursuing army from stopping to gawk at the murdered commander, enabling Joab to maintain military momentum.

gloss_terse: Yagur, a town in southern Judah near Edom (Joshua 15:21)
gloss_readable: This place name designates one of the southernmost cities allotted to the tribe of Judah, positioned in the Negev toward the Edomite border. Like many settlements in this arid region, Yagur appears only in the comprehensive boundary and city lists of Joshua 15, with no further narrative development. The site's exact location remains uncertain to modern archaeologists.

senses.1: A town in the extreme southern territory of Judah, near the border with Edom (Josh 15:21). The name appears in the list of cities allotted to Judah as part of the tribal inheritance, representing one of the frontier settlements in the Negev wilderness.

gloss_terse: Those weary or exhausted in strength (Job 3:17)
gloss_readable: This adjective describes the toil-worn and physically exhausted. Job uses it in his lament over birth, imagining death as a place where 'the weary in strength' finally find rest. The phrase captures those worn down by hard labor and physical exertion, their vitality drained by unceasing toil. The rare construct form adds poetic intensity to Job's vision of death as release from life's burdens.

senses.1: People exhausted from physical labor and hardship, who find rest in death according to Job's bitter meditation (Job 3:17). The expression 'weary of strength' intensifies the image of complete depletion, where even one's physical capacity for exertion has been consumed by relentless labor.

gloss_terse: Jogli, a chief from the tribe of Dan (Numbers 34:22)
gloss_readable: This personal name, possibly meaning 'led into exile' or derived from a root suggesting revelation, belongs to the father of Bukki, who served as Dan's representative in dividing the Promised Land. The name appears only in the formal list of tribal leaders appointed to oversee the land allocation, suggesting Jogli was a recognized ancestral figure whose authority passed to his son.

senses.1: The father of Bukki, who represented the tribe of Dan in the division of Canaan (Num 34:22). Jogli's inclusion establishes his son's tribal authority and genealogical credentials for this crucial administrative role in Israel's inheritance of the land.

gloss_terse: The product or gain from labor (Job 20:18)
gloss_readable: This noun denotes what is acquired through toil and work, the fruit of one's labor. Zophar uses it in his speech about the wicked person's fate, declaring that such a one must restore what he toiled for without swallowing it down. The term appears in parallel with 'exchange' or 'recompense,' emphasizing the economic value of work's product. It captures the material result of exertion rather than the process of working.

senses.1: The material gain or product obtained through hard work, which the wicked must surrender according to Zophar's theology of retribution (Job 20:18). The term emphasizes the tangible results of labor that the unrighteous cannot ultimately enjoy, despite their toil.

gloss_terse: Weariness or exhaustion, especially from study (Ecclesiastes 12:12)
gloss_readable: This late Hebrew noun describes the fatigue that comes from intense mental or physical effort. The Preacher uses it in his epilogue to warn that excessive study wearies the flesh. The word's formation reflects post-exilic Hebrew development, and its single occurrence captures Qoheleth's pragmatic concern about the limits of human intellectual pursuit. Much learning, however valuable, exacts a physical toll.

senses.1: The physical and mental exhaustion produced by prolonged study and intellectual labor (Eccl 12:12). The Preacher's observation that 'much study is a weariness of the flesh' acknowledges the bodily cost of relentless learning, tempering the unlimited pursuit of knowledge with practical wisdom.

gloss_terse: Jegar-Sahadutha, Aramaic name for the witness heap (Genesis 31:47)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic phrase meaning 'heap of witness' or 'witness pile' designates the stone cairn erected by Laban as a covenant marker between himself and Jacob. While Jacob gives the heap a Hebrew name (Galeed), Laban uses this Aramaic expression, reflecting his cultural and linguistic background in Paddan-Aram. The bilingual naming underscores the covenant's role as a boundary between two cultural-linguistic worlds, though both names carry identical meaning.

senses.1: The Aramaic designation Laban gave to the stone heap marking the covenant boundary with Jacob (Gen 31:47). The Aramaic name parallels Jacob's Hebrew 'Galeed,' both meaning 'witness heap,' highlighting how the monument served as a memorial and boundary marker between the two kinsmen's territories.

gloss_terse: Yidalah, a town in Zebulun's territory (Joshua 19:15)
gloss_readable: This place name marks one of the cities allotted to the tribe of Zebulun in the northern hill country. The Septuagint offers variant readings (Jericho in one tradition, Iedalah in Lucianic manuscripts), and the site's precise location remains unknown to archaeologists. Like many Zebulunite settlements, Yidalah receives only this single mention in the territorial boundary lists without further narrative development.

senses.1: A town within Zebulun's tribal inheritance in Galilee (Josh 19:15). The name appears in the list of twelve cities allotted to Zebulun, though its exact location has not been identified in modern archaeological surveys.

gloss_terse: Yidvash, possibly a descendant of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:3)
gloss_readable: This personal name appears in a textually difficult genealogical passage concerning the family of Etam in Judah's lineage. The Masoretic Text's syntax is ambiguous, and the Septuagint interprets these as sons of Aitan rather than following the Hebrew as it stands. Some manuscripts suggest emendations that would clarify Yidvash's genealogical position. The name may derive from a root meaning 'honey' or 'sweetness,' though this remains speculative.

senses.1: An individual listed among the descendants of Judah, though the textual difficulties in 1 Chronicles 4:3 make the exact relationship uncertain. The Septuagint and various textual traditions attempt to clarify this figure's connection to Etam and other family members.

gloss_terse: The beloved one, object of love (Jeremiah 12:7)
gloss_readable: This rare feminine noun denotes not the emotion of love but the person who is loved, the beloved object. God uses it in a lament over abandoning his inheritance, calling Israel 'the beloved of my soul.' The term intensifies the pathos of divine rejection: what was most cherished must now be handed over to enemies. The possessive construction with 'soul' (nephesh) heightens the personal, emotional dimension of God's relationship with his people.

senses.1: Israel as the object of God's deepest affection, 'the beloved of my soul,' whom he must nevertheless deliver into the hands of enemies (Jer 12:7). The term captures the anguished irony of divine judgment: God must abandon the very people he loves most intimately.

gloss_terse: Jadon, a Meronothite who helped rebuild Jerusalem's walls (Nehemiah 3:7)
gloss_readable: This personal name belongs to one of the builders who participated in Nehemiah's restoration of Jerusalem's fortifications. Jadon worked alongside Melatiah the Gibeonite on the section extending to the official seat of the governor of the province Beyond the River. His designation as 'the Meronothite' identifies him by hometown, a settlement whose exact location remains uncertain. The name appears only in this single context.

senses.1: A builder from Meronoth who joined Nehemiah's wall reconstruction project, working on the section near the governor's residence (Neh 3:7). His participation represents the broader community involvement in restoring Jerusalem's defenses beyond the immediate returnees.

gloss_terse: Beloved things or love itself; lovely (Psalm 45:1)
gloss_readable: This feminine plural adjective functions as an abstract noun meaning 'love' or 'lovely things.' The psalm superscription describes the composition as 'a song of loves' or 'a love song,' introducing the royal wedding hymn that follows. While BDB lists this under the entry for the adjective 'beloved,' the plural form here captures the theme and mood of the psalm rather than denoting specific beloved persons.

senses.1: The abstract concept of love or the quality of loveliness, used in the superscription to characterize Psalm 45 as a composition celebrating love (Ps 45:1). The term sets the thematic key for the royal wedding song that extols both bride and groom.

gloss_terse: Yedidah, mother of King Josiah (2 Kings 22:1)
gloss_readable: This feminine personal name means 'beloved' and belongs to the wife of Amon and mother of the reforming king Josiah. She came from Bozkath, a town in the Shephelah of Judah. While the text provides no further information about her character or influence, her name appears in the regal formulae that introduce Josiah's reign, establishing his maternal lineage according to standard Deuteronomistic historical practice.

senses.1: The mother of King Josiah, daughter of Adaiah from Bozkath (2 Kgs 22:1). Her name, meaning 'beloved,' may reflect parental affection or signal divine favor anticipating her son's pivotal role in Judah's religious reforms.

gloss_terse: Jedidiah, 'beloved of Yah,' name given to Solomon (2 Samuel 12:25)
gloss_readable: This theophoric name meaning 'beloved of Yahweh' was given to Solomon by the prophet Nathan after his birth. The naming carries profound theological weight: despite David's sin with Bathsheba and the death of their first child, God's love rests on this second son. The text explicitly states the name was given 'because of Yahweh,' signaling divine election and favor. Though Solomon is known by his other name throughout Scripture, this alternative designation reveals his special covenant status.

senses.1: The prophetic name Nathan gave to Solomon at birth, meaning 'beloved of Yahweh' (2 Sam 12:25). The naming demonstrates God's restorative grace and election of David's son despite the adultery and murder that preceded his conception, marking Solomon as divinely chosen.

gloss_terse: Jidlaph, son of Nahor and brother of Abraham (Genesis 22:22)
gloss_readable: This personal name belongs to one of Nahor's eight sons by his wife Milcah, making him Abraham's nephew. The name's etymology is uncertain, though some suggest a connection to weeping or dripping. Like several of Nahor's sons, Jidlaph represents an Aramean tribal ancestor, though no further biblical narrative develops his lineage. His inclusion in the genealogy establishes the broader kinship network connecting Abraham to Mesopotamian peoples.

senses.1: One of the eight sons of Nahor (Abraham's brother) and Milcah, listed in the genealogy of Genesis 22:22. The name represents an Aramean tribal ancestor, expanding the genealogical connection between Abraham's family and the peoples of Paddan-Aram.

gloss_terse: Burden, lot, or what is given (Psalm 55:22)
gloss_readable: This rare noun, possibly meaning 'what is given' and related to 'lot,' appears in the psalmist's exhortation to cast one's burden upon the Lord. The Targum uses a related Aramaic form in other passages. The term encompasses whatever portion of care, anxiety, or responsibility falls to a person—their 'lot' in life. The verb 'cast' suggests releasing control of one's allotted troubles into God's hands, trusting divine providence to bear what seems unbearable.

senses.1: The burden, care, or anxiety that constitutes one's portion in life, which the psalmist urges should be cast upon Yahweh (Ps 55:22). The term may derive from the concept of a 'lot' or allotted portion, capturing both the inevitability and the weight of life's challenges.

gloss_terse: To become Jewish, convert to Judaism (Esther 8:17)
gloss_readable: This denominative Hithpael verb describes the act of identifying oneself as a Jew or converting to Judaism. It appears in Esther during the reversal of Haman's plot, when fear of the Jews fell upon many peoples and they 'became Jews' or 'declared themselves Jews.' The context suggests both genuine conversion and pragmatic identification with the ascendant Jewish community for protection. This is the only biblical occurrence of this verb form, reflecting the unique diaspora setting where Jewish identity could be adopted or claimed.

senses.1: The act of many non-Jews becoming or declaring themselves Jewish in response to Mordecai's elevation and the fear of Jewish power (Est 8:17). The Hithpael form suggests self-identification, whether through genuine conversion or strategic alignment with the victorious Jewish community.

gloss_terse: Yehud, a town in Dan's territory (Joshua 19:45)
gloss_readable: This place name designates a town allotted to the tribe of Dan, identified with modern Yehudiyeh about eight miles east of Joppa. The name's connection to Judah (Yehudah) is uncertain, though Egyptian sources from the Amarna period mention a place Ia-u-du in this region. The site's location in Dan's coastal territory made it strategically significant, though the text provides no narrative beyond its inclusion in the boundary lists.

senses.1: A town in the tribal allotment of Dan, located in the coastal plain east of Joppa (Josh 19:45). The name may reflect early Judahite settlement or influence in this region before Dan's migration northward, or it may derive from the Egyptian geographical designation.

gloss_terse: Yahdai, a member of Caleb's family (1 Chronicles 2:47)
gloss_readable: This personal name appears in the genealogies of Judah, specifically within Caleb's extended family line. The text's syntax creates some ambiguity about whether Yahdai was a son or more distant descendant. The name's meaning is uncertain, though some suggest it means 'Yah leads' or forms a shortened theophoric construction. Like many names in Chronicles' genealogies, no narrative develops around this individual beyond the genealogical notation.

senses.1: An individual within Caleb's lineage in the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 2:47). The genealogical context provides no additional information beyond establishing Yahdai as part of Caleb's extended family network, typical of Chronicles' comprehensive but compressed tribal records.

gloss_terse: The Jewess, a designation in 1 Chronicles 4:18
gloss_readable: This feminine gentilicial adjective with the definite article designates a woman identified as Jewish or Judahite. In the genealogical passage of 1 Chronicles 4:18, the term appears in a textually difficult verse concerning the descendants of Bithiah, Pharaoh's daughter whom Mered married. The designation 'the Jewess' distinguishes this wife from Bithiah, who was Egyptian. The usage reflects the ethnic-religious identity marker that becomes prominent in post-exilic literature.

senses.1: A woman identified ethnically as Jewish or Judahite, distinguished from Mered's Egyptian wife (1 Chr 4:18). The definite article suggests a specific woman whose Jewish identity was her primary designation in the genealogical record, contrasting her background with the foreign wife.

gloss_terse: Judith, a Hittite wife of Esau (Genesis 26:34)
gloss_readable: This personal name, possibly meaning 'Jewess' or 'woman of Judah' though applied to a Hittite, belongs to one of Esau's wives who caused grief to Isaac and Rebekah. She was the daughter of Beeri the Hittite. The relationship between this name and the gentilicial 'Jewish' is obscure; it may represent a foreign name that coincidentally resembles the Hebrew term. Genesis 36 does not list her among Esau's wives, suggesting either variant traditions or that she died without sons.

senses.1: A Hittite woman, daughter of Beeri, who became one of Esau's wives and brought bitterness to his parents (Gen 26:34). Her marriage represents Esau's pattern of choosing Canaanite wives outside the covenant family line, contributing to the narrative tension between Jacob and Esau.

gloss_terse: Yehukhal, a courtier of King Zedekiah (Jeremiah 37:3)
gloss_readable: This theophoric name, probably contracted from 'Yahweh is able,' belongs to an official in Zedekiah's court. The king sent Yehukhal (whose name appears as Jucal in Jeremiah 38:1) along with the priest Zephaniah to ask Jeremiah to pray for the nation during Babylon's siege. Ironically, the same official later advocated for Jeremiah's death as a defeatist. The name's meaning—celebrating God's power—stands in tension with the bearer's opposition to God's prophetic word.

senses.1: A royal official whom Zedekiah sent to request Jeremiah's intercession, later becoming one of the prophet's accusers (Jer 37:3; 38:1). The name, meaning 'Yah is able,' contrasts with Yehukhal's inability to recognize divine sovereignty in Jeremiah's message of surrender.

gloss_terse: Joseph, here 'in Joseph' as tribal/territorial designation (Psalm 81:5)
gloss_readable: This prepositional phrase uses Joseph's name to denote either the northern kingdom (since Ephraim and Manasseh dominated the north) or the entire people of Israel (with Joseph as representative figure). Psalm 81 recounts the exodus and covenant, and 'in Joseph' likely refers to the whole nation considered through one of the patriarch's names. The usage reflects how Joseph's name could metonymically represent Israel, especially in poetic and prophetic literature.

senses.1: A reference to the people of Israel or the northern tribes, designated through the name of the patriarch Joseph (Ps 81:5). The psalm's exodus context suggests the name functions as a poetic synonym for the covenant people whom God redeemed from Egypt.

gloss_terse: Yehosheva, daughter of Joram who saved Joash (2 Kings 11:2)
gloss_readable: This theophoric name meaning 'Yahweh is an oath' or 'Yahweh has sworn' belongs to the courageous woman who rescued the infant Joash from Athaliah's massacre. She was King Joram's daughter, Queen Ahaziah's sister, and the high priest Jehoiada's wife. Chronicles 22:11 gives the alternate form Yehoshabeath. By hiding the legitimate heir for six years in the temple, Yehosheva preserved the Davidic line and made possible the covenant restoration under her husband's leadership.

senses.1: The daughter of King Joram and wife of the high priest Jehoiada, who rescued the infant Joash from Athaliah's purge and hid him in the temple for six years (2 Kgs 11:2). Her decisive action preserved the Davidic dynasty and enabled the eventual overthrow of Athaliah's illegitimate rule.

gloss_terse: Iob/Job, son of Issachar (Genesis 46:13)
gloss_readable: This personal name appears in the list of Jacob's descendants who went to Egypt, listed as one of Issachar's sons. However, Numbers 26:24, 1 Chronicles 7:1, and the Samaritan Pentateuch read Jashub instead, suggesting textual variation or possible scribal error. The Septuagint supports the reading Iasouph/Iasouḇ, aligning with the alternate tradition. The name's meaning and etymology remain uncertain due to these textual difficulties.

senses.1: A son of Issachar listed among those who descended to Egypt with Jacob (Gen 46:13), though parallel passages read 'Jashub' instead. The textual variants suggest manuscript divergence, with the alternate reading receiving broader support across biblical and versional traditions.

gloss_terse: A stream or watercourse (Jeremiah 17:8)
gloss_readable: This poetic noun designates a flowing stream or brook. Jeremiah uses it to describe the blessed person who trusts in the Lord, pictured as a tree planted by a stream of water. The term appears in parallel with 'water' (mayim), reinforcing the imagery of constant water supply. Unlike a dry wadi that flows only seasonally, this yûḇal provides reliable moisture, enabling the tree to remain green even during drought.

senses.1: A flowing stream or watercourse that provides constant irrigation, used in Jeremiah's metaphor of the righteous person as a well-watered tree (Jer 17:8). The image contrasts with the shrub in the desert, emphasizing reliable divine provision through all seasons.

gloss_terse: Yuval, son of Lamech and inventor of musical instruments (Genesis 4:21)
gloss_readable: This personal name belongs to one of Lamech's sons by Adah, identified as the father of all who handle the lyre and pipe. Yuval represents the origins of musical culture in the Cainite genealogy. His name likely derives from the same root as the noun for 'stream' (yûḇal), though the semantic connection is uncertain. As Jubal in traditional English translations, he stands alongside his brother Jabal (pastoralists) and half-brother Tubal-Cain (metalworkers) as a cultural founder in the antediluvian world.

senses.1: The son of Lamech and Adah, credited as the ancestor of all musicians who play stringed and wind instruments (Gen 4:21). His role in Genesis 4's genealogy represents the development of artistic and musical culture among humanity's earliest generations.

gloss_terse: Yozavad/Jozachar, servant who killed King Joash (2 Kings 12:21)
gloss_readable: This theophoric name meaning 'Yahweh has remembered' belongs to one of the two conspirators who assassinated King Joash of Judah. He was the son of Shimeath the Ammonitess. The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 24:26 calls him Zabad, a shorter form. The assassination came after Joash abandoned the reforms of Jehoiada and shed innocent blood, including Zechariah the prophet. The conspirators' names ironically contain Yahwistic elements while they execute divine judgment on the apostate king.

senses.1: One of King Joash's servants who conspired to murder him in retaliation for killing Zechariah the priest (2 Kgs 12:21; called Zabad in Chronicles). His Yahwistic name contrasts with his maternal Ammonite heritage, reflecting the mixed court of post-exilic Judah.

gloss_terse: Jehoiachin, penultimate king of Judah (Ezekiel 1:2)
gloss_readable: This theophoric name meaning 'Yahweh establishes' belongs to the young king who reigned only three months before Nebuchadnezzar exiled him to Babylon in 597 BC. Ezekiel dates his visions by the years of Jehoiachin's exile, treating him as the legitimate king even after Zedekiah's installation. The name appears in multiple variant forms across biblical books: Jeconiah, Coniah, Jechoniah. Despite his brief reign and exile, Jehoiachin's release from prison after 37 years becomes a sign of hope for the Davidic line's survival.

senses.1: The exiled king of Judah by whose captivity Ezekiel dates his prophetic visions, treating the exile as the starting point of a new era (Ezek 1:2). Though dethroned and imprisoned, Jehoiachin retained legitimacy in exile, and his eventual release symbolized potential restoration for the Davidic dynasty.

gloss_terse: Yukhal/Jucal, official who opposed Jeremiah (Jeremiah 38:1)
gloss_readable: This is the shortened form of Yehukhal (appearing in Jeremiah 37:3), the name of a royal courtier under Zedekiah. The name appears here as Yukhal or Jucal when he is listed among those officials who heard Jeremiah's message of surrender and accused him of treason. The variant spelling likely represents a contracted or colloquial form of the theophoric name. His role shifts from messenger requesting prayer to prosecutor demanding the prophet's death.

senses.1: The contracted form of Yehukhal's name, used when he joins other officials in accusing Jeremiah of weakening the soldiers' morale during Babylon's siege (Jer 38:1). The shortened name appears in the narrative of Jeremiah's arrest and imprisonment in the cistern.

gloss_terse: The Greeks, sons of Javan (Joel 3:6)
gloss_readable: This gentilicial adjective with the definite article refers to the Ionians or Greeks in Joel's oracle against Judah's enemies. The prophet condemns Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia for selling Jerusalem's children to 'the sons of the Greeks,' removing them far from their homeland. The term reflects the Greek presence in Mediterranean slave trade during the Persian and early Hellenistic periods. The Septuagint translates this as 'Hellenes,' confirming the identification with Greek-speaking peoples.

senses.1: The Ionian Greeks to whom Judean and Jerusalemite captives were sold as slaves by Phoenician and Philistine traders (Joel 3:6). The designation emphasizes the geographic and cultural distance of this exile, as children were trafficked far from their ancestral land to Greek-speaking markets.

gloss_terse: Young plant, tender shoot, or sapling (Isaiah 53:2)
gloss_readable: This noun denotes a young plant or sucker growing up from the ground, used metaphorically in Isaiah's Suffering Servant passage. The servant grows up 'like a young plant' and 'like a root out of dry ground,' emphasizing his humble, unimpressive origins. The term suggests vulnerability and lack of obvious vitality—a tender shoot easily overlooked or trampled. The image captures how the servant's appearance belied his significance, fulfilling Isaiah's theme that God's redemptive work comes through unexpected means.

senses.1: A tender young plant or shoot, used metaphorically to describe the Suffering Servant's humble origins and unimpressive appearance (Isa 53:2). The image emphasizes vulnerability and obscurity, contrasting with expectations of a mighty deliverer emerging from strength rather than weakness.

gloss_terse: Yosifyah, father of one of Ezra's companions (Ezra 8:10)
gloss_readable: This theophoric name meaning 'Yah adds' or 'Yah increases' belongs to the father of one of the family heads who returned with Ezra from Babylon. The man's son led 160 males from Bani's descendants on the return journey. Like many names in Ezra's genealogical lists, Yosifyah receives no further narrative development, serving primarily to establish his son's legitimacy and ancestral credentials for participation in the restoration community.

senses.1: The father of a family head who accompanied Ezra from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem, contributing 160 males to the returning community (Ezra 8:10). His name's meaning, 'Yah adds,' appropriately reflects the growth of the restoration community through successive waves of return.
